content: 1. Ceftin tablets and Ceftin oral suspension are not bioequivalent and cannot be substituted on a milligram-per-milligram basis. 2. Before initiating therapy with Ceftin products, it is essential to determine if the patient has a history of hypersensitivity reactions to Ceftin, other cephalosporins, penicillins, or other drugs. 3. Caution should be exercised when administering this product to penicillin-sensitive patients, as cross-hypersensitivity among beta-lactam antibiotics has been documented and may occur in up to 10% of patients with a history of penicillin allergy. 4. If a clinically significant allergic reaction to Ceftin occurs, the drug should be discontinued immediately, and appropriate therapy should be initiated. 5. Severe acute hypersensitivity reactions may require treatment with epinephrine and other emergency measures, such as oxygen, intravenous fluids, intravenous antihistamines, corticosteroids, pressor amines, and airway management, as clinically indicated. 6. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including Ceftin, and can range from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. 7. Antibacterial agents alter the normal flora of the colon, leading to an overgrowth of C. difficile, which produces toxins A and B that contribute to the development of CDAD. 8. Hypertoxin-producing strains of C. difficile can cause increased morbidity and mortality, as these infections may be resistant to antimicrobial therapy and may require colectomy. 9. CDAD should be considered in all patients presenting with diarrhea following antibiotic use, and a careful medical history is necessary, as CDAD can occur over two months after antibiotic administration. 10. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, ongoing antibiotic use not directed against C. difficile may need to be discontinued. Appropriate fluid and electrolyte management, protein supplementation, antibiotic treatment of C. difficile, and surgical evaluation should be instituted as clinically indicated. 11. Prolonged administration of cefuroxime axetil, like other broad-spectrum antibiotics, may result in the overgrowth of nonsusceptible microorganisms. If superinfection occurs, appropriate measures should be taken. 12. Cephalosporins, including cefuroxime axetil, should be used cautiously in patients receiving potent diuretics, as these diuretics may adversely affect renal function. 13. Cefuroxime axetil should be prescribed with caution in individuals with a history of colitis. 14. The safety and effectiveness of cefuroxime axetil have not been established in patients with gastrointestinal malabsorption, as these patients were excluded from clinical trials. 15. Cephalosporins may be associated with a reduction in prothrombin activity, particularly in patients with renal or hepatic impairment, poor nutritional status, prolonged antimicrobial therapy, or those stabilized on anticoagulant therapy. Prothrombin time should be monitored in at-risk patients, and exogenous Vitamin K administered as needed. 16. Prescribing Ceftin in the absence of a proven or strongly suspected bacterial infection or prophylactic indication is unlikely to benefit the patient and increases the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria. 17. Diarrhea is a common side effect of antibiotics and usually resolves when the antibiotic is discontinued. However, watery and bloody stools, with or without stomach cramps and fever, may occur even two or more months after the last dose of the antibiotic. Patients experiencing these symptoms should contact their physician immediately. 18. Ceftin tablets are tolerated by pediatric patients old enough to swallow the tablet whole. However, crushed tablets have a strong, persistent, bitter taste and should not be administered in this manner. Pediatric patients unable to swallow the tablet whole should receive the oral suspension. 19. Complaints about the taste of the oral suspension, which may impair compliance, occurred in 5% of pediatric patients. 20. Patients should be counseled that antibacterial drugs, including Ceftin, should only be used to treat bacterial infections and not viral infections (e.g., the common cold). 21. Patients should be informed that although they may feel better early in the course of therapy, the medication should be taken exactly as directed. Skipping doses or not completing the full course of therapy may decrease the effectiveness of the immediate treatment and increase the likelihood of bacteria developing resistance to Ceftin or other antibacterial drugs in the future. 22. False-negative results may occur in ferricyanide glucose tests; therefore, glucose oxidase or hexokinase methods should be used to determine blood/plasma glucose levels in patients receiving cefuroxime axetil. 23. The presence of cefuroxime does not interfere with the assay of serum and urine creatinine by the alkaline picrate method. 24. Concomitant administration of probenecid with cefuroxime axetil tablets increases the area under the serum concentration versus time curve by 50%. 25. Drugs that reduce gastric acidity may lower the bioavailability of Ceftin compared to the fasting state and negate the effect of postprandial absorption. 26. Like other antibiotics, cefuroxime axetil may affect gut flora, leading to reduced estrogen reabsorption and decreased efficacy of combined oral estrogen/progesterone contraceptives. 27. Lifetime animal studies to evaluate the carcinogenic potential of cefuroxime axetil have not been performed, but no mutagenic activity was found in bacterial mutation tests. 28. Reproduction studies in rats at doses up to 1,000 mg/kg/day (9 times the recommended maximum human dose based on mg/m²) revealed no impairment of fertility. 29. Cefuroxime axetil is classified as Pregnancy Category B. Reproduction studies in mice and rats at high doses revealed no evidence of impaired fertility or harm to the fetus. However, there are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women, so the drug should only be used during pregnancy if clearly needed. 30. Cefuroxime axetil has not been studied for use during labor and delivery. 31. Since cefuroxime is excreted in human milk, consideration should be given to temporarily discontinuing nursing during treatment with cefuroxime axetil. 32. The safety and effectiveness of Ceftin have been established for pediatric patients aged 3 months to 12 years for acute bacterial maxillary sinusitis based on its approval in adults. 33. Use of Ceftin in pediatric patients is supported by pharmacokinetic and safety data in adults and pediatric patients, as well as clinical and microbiological data from adequate and well-controlled studies of acute bacterial maxillary sinusitis in adults and acute otitis media with effusion in pediatric patients. 34. In clinical trials, geriatric patients reported fewer gastrointestinal events and less frequent vaginal candidiasis compared to younger adults, with no clinically significant differences in responses between elderly and younger adult patients. 35. Other clinical experience has not identified differences in responses between elderly and younger adult patients.
